extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists), especially writers of fantasy/adventure interested in using multiple points of view
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for planning, writing, and revising novels that use multiple characters' points of view; includes plot design, casting POV characters, scene-level POV decisions, voice differentiation, and revision strategies. Geared toward writers choosing to adopt or improve multi-POV storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine why you need multiple POVs
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple POV is a choice with consequences — make sure your story really warrants multiple POVs before you start writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't choose multiple POV just because it's harder or because your favorite author uses it. Identify explicit reasons (e.g., cinematic storytelling, exploring unreliability of perspectives). If you can't justify the choice in terms of story needs, consider single POV instead. (The author links to a 'thorough blog post' listing reasons.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Design plot for multiple 'drivers' (single events vs multiple event-sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you'll cover a single set of events from different perspectives or create multiple sets of events that move between places and characters with little overlap coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the approach to match the story/genre: single-event overlapping coverage suits drama/romance/fantasy-of-manners; multiple event-sets suit adventure, action, and mystery. Plan plot structure with the chosen 'driver' approach in mind so POV changes serve the narrative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble an appropriate cast of POV characters (number & necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how many and which POV characters you need; ask why each POV is truly necessary and whether the cast is manageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers new to multi-POV, many coaches recommend no more than three to five POV characters. Don't take on more POVs than you can handle. For each POV, justify its presence by the story function it performs; remove POVs that are redundant or gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give each POV character a complete arc of transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, each POV character should have a complete arc — a mini 'hero's journey' or transformation that justifies their presence as a viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether POV characters will have full arcs or will appear primarily to move the plot along. Prefer giving major POVs their own psychology, goals, and transformation so they feel necessary and resonant rather than mere plot devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whose POV best carries each scene (scene-level POV choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose for every scene which character's POV should carry it — sometimes the best choice is not the character most central to the scene, and not every scene about a character should be in that character's own POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete decision rules such as asking 'Who has the most to lose in this situation?' as a tie-breaker. Consider using another character's POV to shape first impressions (example: meeting a character through someone else's eyes before giving them their own chapter). Be deliberate about scenic choices rather than defaulting to convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each POV character distinct (voice, psychology, mannerisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each POV should read like a living, breathing person: they must talk, behave, react, and think like themselves so that readers can feel genuinely different perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure distinct prose, psychology, style, and voice so readers can tell whose chapter they're in from the writing alone. Aim to evoke empathy even for villains, vary age/naïveté/background where useful, and avoid letting characters blur together. Anti-pattern: characters who are too similar — if they're indistinguishable, collapse them to conserve story space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use POV strategically to create irony, suspense, and dramatic tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple POV enables dramatic effects such as irony and suspense by letting readers hold knowledge that characters do not or by showing conflicting interpretations of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit misunderstandings between characters, layered perspectives, and the ability to withhold or reveal information through selective POV choices to increase narrative tension and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise toward the minimum viable story (POV passes and pruning)
rubrics_metrics.description: During revision, ensure all POVs work in harmony and remove excess material so the final book has no story gaps and no excess baggage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do dedicated 'POV passes' (one or more) to check whether you have all necessary POVs, whether any are missing, if each POV opens in the right place (their own POV or someone else's), and how unique their psychologies/styles are. Revise all POVs together to check cohesion, and also revise each POV separately to sharpen voice. Aim to finish with the smallest set of POVs that accomplish the story goals.
